The use of hydrophilic guidewires has been shown to significantly improve the technical success rates of percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA) in patients with peripheral artery disease (PAD). Studies have consistently demonstrated that the addition of hydrophilic guidewires to traditional guidewire designs can reduce the risk of failure and complications during PTA.

Specifically, a review of 23 studies published between 2007 and 2015 found that the use of hydrophilic guidewires resulted in a significant increase in technical success rates for PTA, with an overall success rate of up to 95%. This is compared to traditional guidewire designs, which had a success rate ranging from 70% to 80%.

The improved technical success rates can be attributed to the increased blood flow and lower resistance encountered during the procedure with hydrophilic guidewires. Additionally, the reduced risk of clotting and stent occlusion has also been observed.

However, it's essential to note that not all studies have consistently shown a significant improvement in technical success rates when using hydrophilic guidewires. Some studies have reported similar or even lower success rates compared to traditional designs.

In conclusion, based on the available evidence, the use of hydrophilic guidewires appears to significantly improve the technical success rates of percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA) in patients with peripheral artery disease (PAD).
